_comment: Hand-maintained annotations that a C header cannot express.
Everything inferable from alpm.h itself (string ownership via const-ness,
handle-ness via incomplete struct types, struct field layout) is NOT
recorded here -- emit.py derives it. This file is only for what clang
genuinely cannot see. Keep it small; if an entry could be a rule, make it
a rule.

rules._comment: Applied in order; first match wins. Overridden by 'functions'.

_comment: Accessors cheap enough to fetch for a whole list at once. They read a
field of an already-loaded db entry, so batching them is free; the
exclusions do real work (hashing a package file, computing a download
size) or are not accessors at all, and must stay one call per use.
Whether an accessor is cheap is not something the header states.
alpm_list_t is untyped in C, so the element type of every list that
crosses the wire has to be stated. Getting one of these wrong is a
type confusion the compiler cannot catch, so they are grouped by
element type rather than alphabetically -- it makes a wrong entry
stand out.
Note the two compute_* functions return package NAMES, not packages,
despite their neighbours in this list returning alpm_pkg_t*.

param_list_elem._comment: Element type of alpm_list_t* parameters, same problem.

record_list_elem._comment: Element type of alpm_list_t* fields inside transparent structs.

alpm_initialize.doc: err is an out-param, not an input.

alpm_release.doc: Invalidates every handle owned by this alpm_handle_t.

alpm_fetch_pkgurl.doc: urls goes in and fetched comes back. Its element type and its caller ownership were already stated; only the direction was missing.

skip._comment: Implemented by hand in arpc_callbacks.c on both sides. Each callback has its own payload shape, so this is six specific things rather than a family the emitter could generate. The ctx getters go with them: the pointer never leaves the client, so there is nothing to ask the server for.

_comment: Empty: the allowlist has served its purpose. Everything the emitter
can generate is now generated, and coverage.json says why the rest
is not.
These free a struct this client materialised, so they must never reach
the server -- it has libalpm's own copy, which it does not own. The
generated stub calls the matching free_<record> helper locally and costs
no round trip.
The value is the record whose free helper to call.
Ownership of a returned struct pointer. Unlike strings, const-ness does
not settle this: both of these return a non-const pointer.
alpm_dep_from_string is documented as newly allocated and freed with
alpm_dep_free; alpm_db_get_group returns the db's own entry.
A variadic function whose `...` the client can format away, and the
name of the format parameter it formats into. The wire cannot carry
`...`, but the client is where the arguments are -- so it formats them
and the text travels. The server then calls libalpm with a literal
"%s" and that text, never with the text as the format.
This is the mirror of logcb, where the server consumes a va_list and
sends what it produced.
A count plus a pointer to N elements, rather than a pointer to one.
The field kinds cannot tell the difference -- `alpm_file_t *files` looks
exactly like a pointer to a single struct -- so which field holds the
count and which holds the array is stated here. The element type comes
off the array field, so it does not need saying twice.
These cross as a plain array; its length is the count.
Records the materialiser must refuse rather than get wrong.
alpm_siglist_t is a counted array too, and that part is now supported.
What still stops it is inside the element: alpm_sigresult_t embeds an
alpm_pgpkey_t by value, whose `data` is the gpgme key itself. Every
other field of that key would cross fine, so this would be a working
function with one silently NULL member -- which is the kind of nearly
right the rest of this generator refuses to produce.
records_unsupported._alpm_siglist_t: element embeds alpm_pgpkey_t, whose data is an opaque gpgme key

_comment: An alpm_list_t** out-param is filled by libalpm and owned by the caller.
The server is that caller, so it frees its copy once serialised; the
client hands the caller a fresh list to free the documented way.
